29:def smoothness(n):
30:    """
31:    Return the B-smooth and B-power smooth values of n.
32:
33:    The smoothness of n is the largest prime factor of n; the power-
34:    smoothness is the largest divisor raised to its multiplicity.
35:
36:    Examples
37:    ========
38:
39:    >>> from sympy.ntheory.factor_ import smoothness
40:    >>> smoothness(2**7*3**2)
41:    (3, 128)
42:    >>> smoothness(2**4*13)
43:    (13, 16)
44:    >>> smoothness(2)
45:    (2, 2)
46:
47:    See Also
48:    ========
49:
50:    factorint, smoothness_p
51:    """
52:
53:    if n == 1:
54:        return (1, 1)  # not prime, but otherwise this causes headaches
55:    facs = factorint(n)
56:    return max(facs), max(m**facs[m] for m in facs)

161:def multiplicity(p, n):
162:    """
163:    Find the greatest integer m such that p**m divides n.
164:
165:    Examples
166:    ========
167:
168:    >>> from sympy import multiplicity, Rational
169:    >>> [multiplicity(5, n) for n in [8, 5, 25, 125, 250]]
170:    [0, 1, 2, 3, 3]
171:    >>> multiplicity(3, Rational(1, 9))
172:    -2
173:
174:    Note: when checking for the multiplicity of a number in a
175:    large factorial it is most efficient to send it as an unevaluated
176:    factorial or to call ``multiplicity_in_factorial`` directly:
177:
178:    >>> from sympy.ntheory import multiplicity_in_factorial
179:    >>> from sympy import factorial
180:    >>> p = factorial(25)
181:    >>> n = 2**100
182:    >>> nfac = factorial(n, evaluate=False)
183:    >>> multiplicity(p, nfac)
184:    52818775009509558395695966887
185:    >>> _ == multiplicity_in_factorial(p, n)
186:    True
187:
188:    See Also
189:    ========
190:
191:    trailing
192:
193:    """
194:    try:
195:        p, n = as_int(p), as_int(n)
196:    except ValueError:
197:        from sympy.functions.combinatorial.factorials import factorial
198:        if all(isinstance(i, (SYMPY_INTS, Rational)) for i in (p, n)):
199:            p = Rational(p)
200:            n = Rational(n)
201:            if p.q == 1:
202:                if n.p == 1:
203:                    return -multiplicity(p.p, n.q)
204:                return multiplicity(p.p, n.p) - multiplicity(p.p, n.q)
205:            elif p.p == 1:
206:                return multiplicity(p.q, n.q)
207:            else:
208:                like = min(
209:                    multiplicity(p.p, n.p),
210:                    multiplicity(p.q, n.q))
211:                cross = min(
212:                    multiplicity(p.q, n.p),
213:                    multiplicity(p.p, n.q))
214:                return like - cross
215:        elif (isinstance(p, (SYMPY_INTS, Integer)) and
216:                isinstance(n, factorial) and
217:                isinstance(n.args[0], Integer) and
218:                n.args[0] >= 0):
219:            return multiplicity_in_factorial(p, n.args[0])
220:        raise ValueError('expecting ints or fractions, got %s and %s' % (p, n))
221:
222:    if n == 0:
223:        raise ValueError('no such integer exists: multiplicity of %s is not-defined' %(n))
224:    return remove(n, p)[1]

1220:def factorint(n, limit=None, use_trial=True, use_rho=True, use_pm1=True,
1221:              use_ecm=True, verbose=False, visual=None, multiple=False):
1222:    r"""
1223:    Given a positive integer ``n``, ``factorint(n)`` returns a dict containing
1224:    the prime factors of ``n`` as keys and their respective multiplicities
1225:    as values. For example:
1226:
1227:    >>> from sympy.ntheory import factorint
1228:    >>> factorint(2000)    # 2000 = (2**4) * (5**3)
1229:    {2: 4, 5: 3}
1230:    >>> factorint(65537)   # This number is prime
1231:    {65537: 1}
1232:
1233:    For input less than 2, factorint behaves as follows:
1234:
1235:        - ``factorint(1)`` returns the empty factorization, ``{}``
1236:        - ``factorint(0)`` returns ``{0:1}``
1237:        - ``factorint(-n)`` adds ``-1:1`` to the factors and then factors ``n``
1238:
1239:    Partial Factorization:
1240:
1241:    If ``limit`` (> 3) is specified, the search is stopped after performing
1242:    trial division up to (and including) the limit (or taking a
1243:    corresponding number of rho/p-1 steps). This is useful if one has
1244:    a large number and only is interested in finding small factors (if
1245:    any). Note that setting a limit does not prevent larger factors
1246:    from being found early; it simply means that the largest factor may
1247:    be composite. Since checking for perfect power is relatively cheap, it is
1248:    done regardless of the limit setting.
1249:
1250:    This number, for example, has two small factors and a huge
1251:    semi-prime factor that cannot be reduced easily:
1252:
1253:    >>> from sympy.ntheory import isprime
1254:    >>> a = 1407633717262338957430697921446883
1255:    >>> f = factorint(a, limit=10000)
1256:    >>> f == {991: 1, int(202916782076162456022877024859): 1, 7: 1}
1257:    True
1258:    >>> isprime(max(f))
1259:    False
1260:
1261:    This number has a small factor and a residual perfect power whose
1262:    base is greater than the limit:
1263:
1264:    >>> factorint(3*101**7, limit=5)
1265:    {3: 1, 101: 7}
1266:
1267:    List of Factors:
1268:
1269:    If ``multiple`` is set to ``True`` then a list containing the
1270:    prime factors including multiplicities is returned.
1271:
1272:    >>> factorint(24, multiple=True)
1273:    [2, 2, 2, 3]
1274:
1275:    Visual Factorization:
1276:
1277:    If ``visual`` is set to ``True``, then it will return a visual
1278:    factorization of the integer.  For example:
1279:
1280:    >>> from sympy import pprint
1281:    >>> pprint(factorint(4200, visual=True))
1282:     3  1  2  1
1283:    2 *3 *5 *7
1284:
1285:    Note that this is achieved by using the evaluate=False flag in Mul
1286:    and Pow. If you do other manipulations with an expression where
1287:    evaluate=False, it may evaluate.  Therefore, you should use the
1288:    visual option only for visualization, and use the normal dictionary
1289:    returned by visual=False if you want to perform operations on the
1290:    factors.
1291:
1292:    You can easily switch between the two forms by sending them back to
1293:    factorint:
1294:
1295:    >>> from sympy import Mul
1296:    >>> regular = factorint(1764); regular
1297:    {2: 2, 3: 2, 7: 2}
1298:    >>> pprint(factorint(regular))
1299:     2  2  2
1300:    2 *3 *7
1301:
1302:    >>> visual = factorint(1764, visual=True); pprint(visual)
1303:     2  2  2
1304:    2 *3 *7
1305:    >>> print(factorint(visual))
1306:    {2: 2, 3: 2, 7: 2}
1307:
1308:    If you want to send a number to be factored in a partially factored form
1309:    you can do so with a dictionary or unevaluated expression:
1310:
1311:    >>> factorint(factorint({4: 2, 12: 3})) # twice to toggle to dict form
